newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: The Philippine Economy from the IMF's Perspective.
newsitem.headline: The Philippine Economy from the IMF's Perspective.

text.p: By David Nellor, IMF Resident Representative, Manila

From my perspective, the most compelling thoughts on the Philippine economy are the extraordinary dramatic transformation of the economy and the credit that should go to the policy makers for securing those gains.
Think of how far the Philippine economy has come over the past decade. Many indicators point to progress. Let me reflect on just one indicator that, in the past, was foremost in everyone's mind.

This indicator, of the debt crisis of the 1980s, is external debt. The external debt-to-GNP ratio has plummeted from a peak of about 100 percent in 1986 to almost half this level in 1996. Similarly, the ratio of debt service to exports of goods and services has plunged about 75 persent from a peak of about 50 percent in 1987 to just 12 percent today. Still, external debt is of course only a symptom.

The domestic policy course set the scene for the debt crisis although external developments were a trigger. The high level of external debt recorded in the mid 1980s was, of course, the legacy of policies dating from the 1970s. The Philippines had embarked on a programme of accelerated growth based on massive investment and public involvement in various industries.

At the same time, substantial trade barriers shielded the economy from external competition. Most of the resources for this investment came from foreign sources, and debt in particular, with limited recourse to domestic savings. The debt crisis halted these external financing flows abruply.

It is against this background that the Philippines embarked on an ambitious programme of reform. The Philippines knows well the importance of seizing the benefits of the global economy and minimizing economic risks through sound macroeconomic policy and strutural reform.
Moreover, the indelible experience of a painful economic history is a strong insurance policy for investors that the ambitious Philippine reform programme is irreversible.

Recent developments reflect just the beginning of the rewards from this reform. Economic expansion has been sustained for a third year helping to lift the Philippines toward the ranks of the fast-growing industrializing countries and paving the way for reduction of poverty.
For 1996, the prospect is that GDP growth will reach 5 1/2 percent, buoyed by faster growth in manufacturing and services, and a recovery in agriculture.

Recorded remittances have increased substantially, spurring GNP growth to about seven percent. There are few indications of major capacity constraints or bottlenecks and certainly none on the scale of the power shortage that thwarted recovery in the early 1990's.

In these circumstances, further expansion in output can be envisaged without rekindling inflation, if wages and other costs are contained. Indeed, the recovery of agricultural supply in 1996 and the overall policy framework have ensured the rapid decline in inflation, expected to be about six percent by December.
However, domestic demand expansion-from both investment and consumption-is likely to exceed GDP growth and is associated with some widening in the trade deficit.
A substantial inflow of remittances and an increasing capital account surplus is financing this deficit. Indeed, foreign exchange reserves are projected to remain well above target.

The Government has maintained prudent fiscal and monetary policies in 1996. The Government is achieving fiscal goals though there are ongoing difficulties in tax collections, completing the privatization programme, and sustaining the planned pace of expenditure on much needed capital projects.

This experience underscores the vital need for further fiscal balance. The firm stance of monetary policy is appropriate with the widening of the trade deficit and the challenge of keeping inflation close to the targeted path.

The challenge now is to extend the track record of sound macroeconomic policy, to raise sustainable economic growth, and to strengthen the economy to withstand inevitable shocks. The economy has already exhibited greater resilience than in years past.

Witness the developments in 1995 - the Mexico shock early in the year and then the rice crisis. In the past, either of these developments may have been sufficient to derail the economy yet last year economic growth accelerated as the year progressed. To repeat my theme, it is now time to strengthen the economy to raise sustainable growth and increase the resiliency of the economy.
This objective presents a daunting task for policy makers. Two reasons come to mind: defining the policy course is difficult and so is explaning the need for that policy stance.

Let me elaborate. First, the prescription may be difficult to define. When, for example, inflation is high or the fiscal deficit is out of control, the prescription for alleviating the economic dislocation is straightforward even if sometimes politically demanding.

The task now is quite different, it is to fine tune policies, introduce measures that will promote high and sustainable economic growth, and to avoid the costs of economic shocks. Identifying such measures is not always easy -- after all, accurately foreseeing the nature of economic shocks is impossible by definition.

Nevertheless, identifying such policy requirements is extremely important to sustain high economic growth. The second difficulty is to explain, to the general population, the need for policy measures when economic conditions have already improved so markedly.
For example, some ask, why is tax reform needed when the fiscal position is so strong?

I will answer this question shortly. Let me note now, however, that the strong political leadership that has delivered the dramatic economic gains in recent years becomes even more important in securing passage of economic policy in this new economic environment.
What then are some challenges? Today I will briefly outline three issues; building national savings, strengthening competitiveness, and promoting a strong financial sector.
Each of these is a major topic on its own but let me just sketch some issues focusing mainly on national savings.
BUILDING NATIONAL SAVINGS

National savings is a critical ingredient to elevate the rate of sustainable economic growth without jeopardizing macroeconomic stability. In the 1970s and 1980s, domestic saving was chronically low, impeding the country's growth performance. Increased investment was reflected in higher current account deficits financed by resort to debt that exposed the economy to risk. These earlier economic recoveries inevitably ran out of energy and particularly if they did not produce an increase in economic productivity but were boosted by consumption. Foreign savings plays an important role but, ideally, should be limited to a level that autonomous capital flows can finance.

How will national savings be increased? Private savings are low in the Philippines compared to neighbouring countries. The finance industry plays a pivotal role by providing new vehicles for private savings. But, in many countries, the experience is that private savings tend not to increase at the outset of a period of financial sector liberalization. Consequently, public savings by increases in revenue and by reorienting expenditure toward investment.

As a point of comparison, public savings was about 3 percent of GDP in the Philippines, 7 percent of GDP in Indonesia, and 12 to 13 percent of GDP in Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand on average between 1991 and 1995.

In essence, the agenda for increasing public savings in the Philippines today is to pass the government's tax reform and civil service streamlining legislation. As it is so topical, let me take the opportunity to look at the critical role of the comprehensive tax reform package (CTRP). Tax reform is required to consolidate the present fiscal position even before tackling the more ambitious goal of improving national savings.
Timely action is imperative because, without revenues that would accrue from the CTRP, the public sector deficit would widen again in 1997 despite a continued buoyant economy.
Several developments influence budgetary prospects.

* Non-recurrent factors notably privatization receipts have generated recent fiscal improvement. These have accounted for about 1.5 percent of GNP over the past couple of years and, for the short term, are largely exhausted.
* Some fortuitous developments have aided the improved fiscal outturn such as shortfalls in capital outlays by government and public corporations particularly the National Power Corporation.

* The medium-term revenue losses from the programmed tariff reform will be significant. Tariff revenues accounted for as much as 36 percent of tax revenues as recently as 1993. Under the government's tariff reduction program, by 2004, the maximum standard tariff rate will decline from the current 30 percent to 5 percent. While strong import growth could mitigate the impact of tariff reform, the medium term revenue losses from this reform will nevertheless be significant.

* The growing transfer from the national government to local government units (LGUs) is a risk to the national fiscal position although the principle of devolution of some public expenditure responsibilities is entirely appropriate. The decline in tariff revenues increases the risk to the national government expenditure. The 1991 local government code specifies that national government transfers 40 percent of domestic revenues of the three preceding years to local government. Tariff reform means that domestic taxes will increase in importance in the total tax take thereby leading to even more rapid growth of transfer to local government.

* Unless government adjust fees and charges in line with prices, their contribution to revenues as a share of GNP will fall. Discretionary measures to increase fees and chrages are not always easy to introduce.

To summarize, inaction will be costly -- privatization in particular has provided a window of opportunity that the government is looking to seize, via tax and expenditure reform, to lock in the gains that have accrued. But, as noted, fiscal reform must do more than just maintain the status quo in the fiscal accounts; permitting higher rates of economic growth is neccesary while preserving macroeconomic stability. There are three main reasons.

The first point is that tax reform must raise public savings. I have covered the importance of increasing public savings for raising sustainable growth and preserving macroeconomic stability. It is perhaps worth noting why this increase in public savings probably has to rely largely on the revenue side of the budget. Public expenditure is not high in the Philippines despite the importance of private sector involvement in infrastructure development. Another constraint, however, is that tha expenditure side of the budget offers little scope for adjustment. The combination of personal expenditures, interest payments, and the legislated transfers to LGU's accounts for almost three quarters of public outlays and most current outlays.

The second point is that tax reform enables much-needed increase in outlays on infrastructure. Expansion of the private sector needs to be matched by an increase in government spending on physical infrastructure--such as roads, power, and water -- and on human capital--such as health and education. Without these investments, the productivity of private investment is limited and so is the growth rate that can be sustained. To begin to reduce the backlog of unmet infrastructure needs, investment spending must be stepped up.

Of course, the necessary level of public investment depends on the overall economic strategy. In countries where the public sector provides nearly all the required infrastructure, public investment will naturally be higher than in those--such as the Philippines--where the private sector plays an important role. Still, the gap between public infrastructure spending in the Philippines and its ASEAN neighbors is too large to be explained solely by different economic roles of the state. On average, capital expenditure in ASEAN countries was about two percentage points of GDP higher than in the Philippines over the period 1990-93. You will find that the average level of central government capital expenditure is about 5.3 percent of GDP in the main ASEAN countries and the range of this ratio is about 3 percent of GDP to almost 9 percent of GDP. The Philippines is presently at the lower end of this range.

As I have noted, it is not possible to determine the precise capital expenditure needs of any country. Nevertheless, in a recent paper, a colleague and I illustrate the substantial scale of public capital or infrastructure needs in the Philippines. Without suggesting that this is a desirable target, we find that the Philippines would need to double its present rate of national government investment each year for a ten-year period to close the gap with Thailand's public capital stock. We estimate the national government capital stock using budgetary capital spending over an extended period.
Allowing for a moderate rate of depreciation, the stock of national government capital is about US$268 per person in the Philippines.

Compare this with Thailand--the next lowest capital spender. National government investment averaged 3.9 percent of GNP in Thailand over the same period yielding an estimated national government capital stock of about US$757 per person at end 1995. This means that the stock of capital is about $500 per person higher in Thailand than the Philippines. The accumulated shortfall of about US$500 per person represents a diferrence of some US$33 billion in national government investment.

To close the gap--between per capital public capital stock in the Philippines and Thailand--in the next ten years, the Philippine national government investment would need to equal about US$5.3 billion per year at current exchange rates, or double its current level. This is a conservative estimate because these figures assume no relative growth in population.

The third reason for tax reform is to reduce interest rate on a sustainable basis. The public finances need to be placed on a solid ground to assure global financial markets that there will be no return to the days of financial instability. Once this is done, the risk premia on the Philippine assets will fall, allowing interest rates to decline, not just for a few months, but on a long-lasting basis.

The budget has benefited from the recent favorable dynamics of improved budget balance and lower interest rates. Yet, the same virtuous circle could become a vicious circle if favorable interest rate trends were to reverse perhaps due to untoward developments in the world economy. Domestic debt, which accounts for more than half the stock of debt and nearly four-fifths of interest payments, is mostly short-term, making the budget position sensetive to shifts in investor confidence.
Moreover, the large share of resources devoted to paying interest hampers the flexibility of the national government to respond to economic shocks or to increase spending on priority items.
STRENGTHENING COMPETITIVENESS

A second policy challenge for elevating growth and resiliency of the economy is to strengthen competitiveness. In recent months, there has been considerable discussion throughout thr region about weakening export performance and widening trade balance. I do not intend to examine all of the aspects of this development today, but to focus on one critical theme. The theme is that competitiveness of the Philippines export sector will be improved by changes in "real" factors--there are no quick fix solutions. Reflecting this consideration, the government has established the National Action Agenda for Productivity to address these issues. The agenda identities a series of policy measure in the agricultural, industry, and public sectors.

I do not propose to itemize these policies today but rather, at a general level, identify some of these real factors can enhance competitiveness via productivity improvement in the export sector and in competition with imports.

I have already mentioned one important factor that will improve competitiveness, namely infrastructure. The fiscal reforms that can deliver infrastructure will enhance performance in a wide range of sectors. These sectors include, for example, the agriculture sector, tourism, the buoyant electronics sector, and other areas of manufacturing.

The tariff reforms already underway can play an important role in enhancing export competitiveness. They also help ensure domestic producers are using the latest technology and, because they have to complete with the best in the world, are adopting best practices. Other means of helping technology transfer are also important. Likewise simple but important areas of reform include improving further the efficiency of the customs and movement toward an invoice-based valuation system.

Capital market development that helps strong financial intermediation also plays a role in improving Philippines competitiveness. In this sector, development of a domestic corporate debt market, a growing stock market with extensive listing, and development of savings vehicles such as mutual funds are important examples. These and other capital market activities have enormous potential in the Philippines and can make a major contribution to the Government's policy goals.
PROMOTING A STRONG FINANCIAL SECTOR

A third policy challenge is to strengthen the financial sector, as a conduit to productive use of domestic savings and foreign finance, and to ensure it is robust. Just as investment in agriculture is important to make that sector more resistant and resilient to variable and sometimes difficult weather conditions building a financial system that can withstand adverse "economic typhoons" is equally important.

Here I would like to make some comments about all emerging markets and not on the Philippines direcly. A recent IMF study found that since 1980, more than two third of IMF member countries have experienced significant banking sector problems. These countries include all categories of countries from the most sophisticated industrial countries to the least developd countries.

Managing large capital flows in a world of freer capital movements and increasingly integrated international financial markets has become a major challenge for policy makers and bank supervisors. As the financial system has become internationalized and banks have increased their exposure to credit and market risk in the international arena, the dual relationship between macroeconomic policies and banking system weakness has become apparent. As a result, prudential and macroeconomic policies need to be designed to take account of the banking system's capacity to intermediate capital flows efficiently.
At the same time, objectives for banking system soundness need to be considered along with monetary, exchange rate, and fiscal policy objectives in the countext of an open capital account.

Banks, and the finance sector more generally, play key roles in the economy, including mobilization of savings, intermediation, maturity transformation, facilitation of payments flows, credit allocation, and maintenance of borrower financial discipline. Even in economies with highly developed financial markets, banks remain at the center of financial and economic activity, acting as primary providers of payments services and as a fulcrum for monetary policy impementation. In countries with less fully developed financial markets, banks are typically the only institutions able to produce the information necessary for intermediation, to provide the porfolio diversification for maturity transformation and risk reduction, and to help monitor corporate governance.

Policy toward financial institutions is unusual when contrasted with policy toward other sectors of the economy. Because of the central role of financial institutions in the economy, government activity monitors developments and, in extreme circumstances, may intervene to avoid bank failures or to protect depositors. This different treatment of the financial sector, compared with other enterprises, reflects the fact that if financial sector problems are left unattended they could pose a threat to the macroeconomy. The challenge for policy makers is to prevent stress in the system as a whole, while permitting individual institutions to be subject to the rigors of market forces.

In this context, the Bangko Sentral Ng Pilipinas is presently reviewing the General Banking Act. Part of that extensive review involves assessing the need for new guidelines on the capital adequacy of banks. The governor of the BSP recently referred to the possibility of increasing the capital requirements of the banks. These developments reflect a timely and judicious assessment of the requirements for a strong Philippine financial sector.

Let me draw some of these themes together. The Philippines is now in its third year of economic recovery. Economic growth is accelerating and inflation has resumed its downward path. The Philippines is likely to register growing investor interest as it stays the course with the sound policy of recent years and builds a track record of strong macroeconomic policy. In this regard, the markets are unrelenting, sound macroeconomic policy must be perserved with day by day to biuld such a track record--there is no quick-fix substitute. The Philippines is steady passing the milestones that will produce such a complelling track record.

The challenge facing the Philippines now is to take the next step, to build a policy framework that will sustain high economic growth and strengthen the resilience of the economy. This is a challenging task. Defining the economic reforms is sometimes difficult as it involves building safety valves into the economy and addressing unpredictable economic developments. Moreover, economic conditions have improved and it becomes more difficult to explain the payoff to reforms that, on occasion, may be politically difficult.

These challenges facing the Philippine policy makers include building national savings, strengthening international competitiveness, and promoting a strong financial sector. The authorities have embarked on ambitious reforms in each of these areas. The IMF will continue to collaborate with the Philippine authorities on these questions, drawing on international experience and pursuing its role of promoting quality economic growth and a stable international financial system. The quality of the reform efforts of the reform efforts of the past three years engenders every confidence that the Philippine authorities will also be able to declare victory in this next policy challenge.
